text: Renal registry.  This dataset contains nationwide anonymized hospital discharge records of patients diagnosed with Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD; ICD-10 codes N18.1–N18.5) in Ecuador, covering a 10-year period from 2015 to 2024. The database compiles key demographic variables (age, sex, ethnicity, rural/urban residence), institutional metrics (public vs. private healthcare sector, length of stay), ICD-10 clinical severity stages, and in-hospital mortality outcomes. Designed for epidemiological research, statistical modeling (multinomial and binary logistic regression), and health policy analysis, this repository provides curated data to evaluate sociodemographic disparities, clinical progression, and predictors of mortality in hospitalized CKD populations.

title: Central American glaucoma: a comparative review of Honduras against the rest of the region, with supporting Latin American literature (January 1, 2020 to July 30, 2026)
journal: Ramos Espinal, Marco Antonio, Ramos  Licona, Marco Antonio
text: Central American glaucoma: a comparative review of Honduras against the rest of the region, with supporting Latin American literature (January 1, 2020 to July 30, 2026).   Background: glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, yet its burden in Central America,  and specifically how Honduras compares with its neighboring countries, remains almost entirely undocumented in indexed scientific literature. Objective: to characterize the published evidence on glaucoma in Honduras and the rest of Central America between January 1, 2020 and July 30, 2026, comparing findings across the region against the broader Latin American literature available for reference. Methods: multiple rounds of searches were run across PubMed, Scopus (verified indirectly), SciELO, Honduran and Central American medical journals, and regional open-access databases, in Spanish and English, without restricting to a single glaucoma subtype and with a 2020 publication floor. After the initial search revealed an almost total absence of Central American angle-closure glaucoma studies, the scope was broadened twice with the author's explicit authorization: first to Latin America while keeping the angle-closure focus, and then, given similarly scarce results, to glaucoma in general. Results: 15 verifiable sources within the period were confirmed: 4 directly concerning Central America (2 from Costa Rica, 1 from El Salvador, 1 from Honduras), 7 from other Latin American countries (Peru, Colombia, Argentina, Paraguay, Brazil), and 4 systematic reviews or disease-burden analyses of global or regional scope. None of the three systematic reviews identified,  two glaucoma-specific, one on blindness and low vision, reported a single Central American primary study. Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua, and Panama registered no clinical or epidemiological glaucoma study published within the period; Costa Rica and El Salvador contributed limited evidence, mostly narrative or administrative in nature. Discussion: the Honduras-versus-rest-of-Central-America comparison that motivated this work could not be carried out in the sense originally intended, because the comparison term,  Honduran glaucoma research, is, as far as this search can establish, nonexistent; the study's main finding is that absence itself. Conclusions: Central America constitutes a glaucoma research gap consistently documented across regional and international literature, and Honduras is not an exception within that gap but its most complete expression. Priority lines for primary research in the country are proposed.

title: Integrating Traditional Knowledge Systems into Geriatric Care: The Behavioral Philosophy of Yagya
text: Integrating Traditional Knowledge Systems into Geriatric Care: The Behavioral Philosophy of Yagya.     Modern healthcare often addresses aging and lifestyle disorders through purely external interventions, frequently overlooking the inner dimensions of human behavior and consciousness. This article explores the ancient Indian philosophical concept of        Yagya        as a multidimensional framework for holistic health and healthy aging. Beyond its traditional physical rituals,        Yagyagni        (the fire of        Yagya       ) imparts profound behavioral teachings, such as diligent action, minimalist consumption, and altruistic distribution that directly counteract the lethargy and over-consumption driving cardiometabolic and psychological decline. By adopting these practical, psychological tools into daily routines, individuals can foster the behavioral shifts necessary for maintaining cognitive and physical vitality. Ultimately, integrating these philosophical interventions into routine patient care promotes a paradigm shift from technocratic disease management to the internal, ethical transformation of the individual.

title: napari: a multi-dimensional image viewer for Python
journal: Sofroniew, Nicholas, Lambert, Talley, Bokota, Grzegorz
text:
napari: a multi-dimensional image viewer for Python.  napari 0.9.0 
 ⚠️  Note: these release notes are still in draft while 0.9.0rc1 is in prerelease testing.  ⚠️ 
  Thu, Aug 20, 2026  
 We're happy to announce the release of napari 0.9.0!
napari is a fast, interactive, multi-dimensional image viewer for Python.
It's designed for browsing, annotating, and analyzing large multi-dimensional
images. It's built on top of Qt (for the GUI), vispy (for performant GPU-based
rendering), and the scientific Python stack (numpy, scipy). 
 For more information, examples, and documentation, please visit our website,
https://napari.org. 
 napari follows  EffVer (Intended Effort Versioning) ; this is a  Macro  release containing awesome new features, but may require dedication of some significant time when upgrading projects to use this version. 
 Highlights 
 Auto-labelling of viewer axes 
 napari 0.5.0 laid the ground work for more accurate metadata handling by
allowing users and plugins to set the  axis_labels  on layers. napari 0.9.0
 finally  capitalises on that work by automatically labelling viewer axes based
on the axis labels of layers present in the viewer.
( #9282 ) 
 Now, opening a dataset with labelled axes will result in correctly labelled
axes in the viewer: 
 ] 
 Additionally, when you create a new layer from an existing one using the
buttons in the GUI, the new layer now inherits the axis labels of the layer(s)
it was derived from. ( #9293 ) 
 There is still work to be done here. For example, if layers have labels that
are inconsistent with each other, napari will simply ignore layers with fewer
dimensions, or layers added later. But, for most use cases, layer and viewer
metadata will now be much more informative! 
 Layer controls for multiple selected layers 
 Until now, layer controls only appeared when a single layer was selected. Now,
napari dynamically builds the layer controls from your selection, so
when you select several layers at once you can see and use the controls that
are shared between them. Pan-zoom is always available, while the layer-specific
buttons still appear only when a single layer is selected.
( #9318 ) 
 There's also an experimental setting,  Generate GUI layer controls dynamically
instead of using premade panels , that makes napari use the new dynamic
controls even for single layers. 
 Xarray metadata is now inherited 
 If you work with  Xarray  — common in climate,
geoscience, and many places where data ships with labelled coordinates — napari
now reads metadata straight from your  DataArray s. When you add an xarray
object to the viewer, napari will use its dimension names as axis labels, infer
 scale  and  translate  from the coordinate values, and pick up  units  from
CF-convention  units  attributes on coordinates ( #9316 ).
This closed an 8-year old issue:  #14 ! 
 Status bar coordinates as floats 
 Continuing on the theme of improved metadata, when scale and/or unit metadata
is set on the layer, the status bar coordinates now have increased precision,
where before they were limited to just integers. This means you can have more
accurate physical estimates of your data coordinates when exploring data.
( #9287 ) 
 Take a guided tour of the viewer 
 New to napari, or just want a quick refresher on where everything lives? There's
now a guided tour, available from  Help → Take a tour . The tour highlights
the main areas of the viewer — the canvas, the layer list, layer controls, the
viewer buttons, the dimension sliders, and the status bar — so you can get your
bearings in seconds. If the viewer is empty, napari opens the built-in  Balls 
(3D) sample data so the walkthrough has something to show ( #9290 ). 
 Contributable plugin preferences 
 Plugins can now ship their own preferences ( #9308 )!
By declaring  configurations  in
their  napari.yaml  manifest, plugins get their own settings — stored
separately from napari's own settings, automatically added to and editable from
the napari  Preferences  dialog, and accessible programmatically from Python: 
  from napari.settings import get_plugin_settings

settings = get_plugin_settings("my-plugin")
settings.reader.lazy = True
  
 Read more in the  Configurations Guide 
to learn more about how to add this new contribution to your own plugins. 
 Adjust grid rendering with hidden layers 
 Speaking of grid mode: grid mode with hidden layers is much improved: empty
grid spaces are never shown and stride operates on the  full  layer list, so
layer grouping doesn't change when you show or hide layers ( #9244 ). 
 Fuzzy find in command palette 
 Have you used our  command palette  yet? It's a great way to
quickly access and even discover napari functionality. Now, thanks to
 #8661 , it's easier to find
functions when you don't know the exact name, or you mistyped something. You'll
need to have  rapidfuzz  installed to
make use of it. It's automatically installed with  napari[all]  or
 napari[optional] . And if the search feels a bit off, you can set just how
fuzzy you want it to be in Preferences > Experimental > Fuzzy Search Threshold. 
 [screenshot or movie to be provided by Lorenzo] 
 2D slicing of surfaces 
 Ever since we added surfaces, they have been invisible in 2D slices. Now,
thanks to all the work done on  thick slicing , surface
slices appear in 2D view ( #8783 ).
This enhancement is accompanied by support for async slicing, which should
improve viewer responsiveness when slicing large, time varying surfaces, for
example. 
 [movie of ND-cows and slicing] 
 ... And you can try this out yourself with common .obj surface files thanks to
a new built-in reader plugin!
( #9228 ) 
 You should now be able to drag and drop .obj files into napari and see them
instantly. 
 Public API for auto contrast limit 
 For a very long time, it's been possible to set automatic contrast limits
updating on a layer  only  through the graphical user interface. This means an
extra click for many workflows and poorer reproducibility. Thanks to
 #9271 , you can now set the
 auto_contrast  attribute on Image layers: 
  image_layer = viewer.add_image(..., auto_contrast=True)
# or
image_layer.auto_contrast = True
  
 The life-changing magic of tidying up the Viewer model 
 The napari Viewer model, for historical reasons, is a grab-bag of  many 
attributes, which makes usage, discoverability, and code modularity and
composability a major issue. We've taken some  big  steps towards cleaning up
one of our most important namespaces by creating Canvas
( #8633 ) and Scene
( #9323 ) models, which cleans up
( #9363 ) and clarifies
( napari/docs#1083 ) many parts of
the API. 
 The old API is in extremely widespread use, so although it is silently
deprecated, it will continue to work for the foreseeable future. In the
meantime, the new API should be much friendlier to work with by carefully
grouping related concepts and APIs. Some examples: 
 
  viewer.axes  and  viewer.floating_axes  become  viewer.scene.overlays.axes 
and  viewer.canvas.overlays.axes . 
 From that API, you may also guess that the scale bar is on
 viewer.canvas.overlays.scale_bar . 
 You can even get a list of the current overlays (both visible and invisible)
with  list(viewer.canvas.overlays)  and  list(viewer.scene.overlays) . (But
do note that overlays with a  _  prefix are private and may change!) 
  viewer.camera  is now  viewer.scene.camera . 
 Grid mode is now accessed at  viewer.canvas.grid  (e.g.
 viewer.canvas.grid.enabled = True ). 
 
 This has also enabled a new public API: you can now query the canvas size (in
pixels) without accessing private napari APIs! Check  viewer.canvas.size ! 
 The TL;DR: 
  # Canvas Model
viewer.scale_bar -> viewer.canvas.overlays.scale_bar
viewer.text_overlay -> viewer.canvas.overlays.text
viewer.floating_axes -> viewer.canvas.overlays.axes
viewer.grid -> viewer.canvas.grid
NOW EXPOSED -> viewer.canvas.overlays.current_slice
NEW -> viewer.canvas.overlay_tiling
NEW -> viewer.canvas.background_color & viewer.canvas.background_color_override
NEW -> viewer.canvas.size

# Scene Model
viewer.camera -> viewer.scene.camera
viewer.axes -> viewer.scene.overlays.axes
  
 Removal of translation code 
 Several years ago, we started working on implementing localization machinery
into napari. Unfortunately, this work has been sitting unfinished and unused,
while making maintaining napari harder. Given the extra maintenance burden
without benefit, we made the difficult decision to remove it from our codebase
( #8935 ), with the hope that in
the future we might restart this effort with a better plan. 
 We do aim to revisit when napari's foundations are more solid, but for now,
 napari.utils.translations  is deprecated. If you have this code in your
codebase: 
  from napari.utils import translations as trans
  
 please remove it. (For now,  trans._()  is a no-op.)

title: Estratégias psicológicas e odontológicas no manejo comportamental de crianças com Transtorno do Espectro Autista: revisão de literatura
journal: Cunha, Júlia Braga, Matos Junior, Ercs John Dias, Silva, Janaína Elena
text: Estratégias psicológicas e odontológicas no manejo comportamental de crianças com Transtorno do Espectro Autista: revisão de literatura.  O Transtorno do Espectro Autista (TEA) caracteriza-se por alterações na comunicação social, padrões comportamentais restritos e hipersensibilidades sensoriais que podem dificultar significativamente o atendimento odontológico infantil. Diante disso, o presente estudo teve como objetivo reunir e analisar evidências científicas acerca das estratégias psicológicas e odontológicas utilizadas no manejo comportamental de crianças com TEA durante o atendimento odontológico, com enfoque na integração entre cirurgiões-dentistas e psicólogos. Trata-se de uma revisão integrativa da literatura, realizada nas bases SciELO, PubMed, BIREME, SciSpace e Connected Papers, incluindo estudos publicados entre 2016 e 2026, nos idiomas português e inglês. Foram analisadas estratégias como Análise do Comportamento Aplicada (ABA), dessensibilização sistemática, reforço positivo, comunicação alternativa, suporte visual e adaptações ambientais do consultório odontológico. Os resultados demonstraram que abordagens individualizadas e interdisciplinares favorecem a cooperação da criança, reduzem a ansiedade e a resistência ao tratamento e contribuem para experiências clínicas mais humanizadas e eficazes. Além disso, observou-se que a participação familiar e o preparo prévio da criança desempenham papel fundamental no sucesso terapêutico. Apesar dos avanços encontrados, a literatura ainda apresenta limitações metodológicas, como heterogeneidade dos estudos e ausência de padronização das intervenções. Conclui-se que a associação entre estratégias psicológicas e odontológicas representa importante ferramenta para promoção da saúde bucal e inclusão de crianças com TEA no cuidado odontológico.

title: From hope to heartbreak: supporting women through repeated fertility treatment failure: A narrative review of the role of infertility nurses
text: From hope to heartbreak: supporting women through repeated fertility treatment failure: A narrative review of the role of infertility nurses.  Background: Infertility and assisted reproductive treatment can be emotionally demanding experiences. Although advances in assisted reproductive technology have improved opportunities for conception, repeated unsuccessful fertility treatment may result in considerable psychological, social, relational, and emotional distress. Women undergoing repeated in-vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles may experience anxiety, grief, hopelessness, self-blame, social isolation, and uncertainty regarding future treatment. The emotional burden may become particularly pronounced after repeated embryo-transfer failures. Aim: This narrative review aims to explore the emotional and psychosocial impact of repeated fertility treatment failure among women and to describe the role of infertility nurses in providing supportive, evidenceinformed, and patient-centred care. Methods: A narrative review approach was used to examine published literature and professional recommendations concerning recurrent implantation failure, infertility-related psychological distress, and psychosocial care during assisted reproductive treatment, patient communication, and nursing support. Relevant literature was identified through PubMed/MEDLINE and guidance from the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE). Recent literature concerning the psychosocial consequences of recurrent implantation failure was also considered. Results: Repeated fertility treatment failure may be associated with anxiety, grief, reduced hope, emotional exhaustion, social withdrawal, relationship difficulties, and concerns about continuing treatment. Patients may also experience self-blame and uncertainty about whether their actions contributed to treatment failure. Current ESHRE recommendations emphasize individualized assessment, compassionate communication, adequate time for discussion, honest information regarding prognosis, shared decision-making, and access to psychosocial care. Infertility nurses have an important role in identifying emotional distress, providing therapeutic communication and education, facilitating communication with fertility specialists, supporting coping, and arranging referral to mental-health professionals when required. Conclusion: The consequences of repeated fertility treatment failure extend beyond reproductive outcomes. Psychosocial care should be integrated into routine infertility nursing practice. Nurses can contribute significantly by providing empathetic communication, emotional assessment, evidence-based education, continuity of care, and timely referral. Supporting women through repeated treatment failure should be considered an essential component of quality infertility care rather than an optional service.

title: Effectiveness of structured teaching programme on knowledge regarding surgical site infection and its prevention among staff nurses
journal: Shivank Maheshwari, Dr. Anitha Martin, L. Priyalata Devi
text: Effectiveness of structured teaching programme on knowledge regarding surgical site infection and its prevention among staff nurses.  Surgical site infection (SSI) is one of the most common healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) worldwide, contributing significantly to increased patient morbidity, prolonged hospital stays, escalating healthcare costs, and, in severe cases, mortality. Global estimates indicate that the pooled cumulative incidence of SSI among general surgical patients is approximately 11%, meaning that roughly one in every nine to ten patients undergoing surgery may develop an infection at the operative site within thirty days of the procedure. In India, reported SSI rates vary widely from 4.2% to 38% depending on the type of surgery, hospital setting, and surveillance methodology used. Staff nurses, being present at every stage of the perioperative continuum, play a pivotal role in preventing surgical site infections through consistent adherence to evidencebased infection prevention and control practices. Objectives: To evaluate the effectiveness of a structured teaching programme (STP) on knowledge regarding surgical site infection and its prevention among staff nurses, and to determine the association between pre-test knowledge scores and selected socio-demographic variables. Materials and Methods: A quantitative, preexperimental, one-group pre-test–post-test research design was adopted. The study was conducted among 50 staff nurses at Rohilkhand Medical College & Hospital, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh, selected through non-probability convenience sampling. Data were collected using a selfstructured, validated knowledge questionnaire and analyzed using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS), version 20. Results: The findings revealed a statistically significant improvement in the knowledge of staff nurses regarding surgical site infection and its prevention following the structured teaching programme, with the mean knowledge score rising from 14.06 ± 4.492 in the pre-test to 22.89 ± 2.674 in the post-test (paired t = 24.255, p = 0.0001), an absolute gain of 8.83 points and a relative improvement of approximately 62.8%. A statistically significant association was also found between pre-test knowledge scores and selected socio-demographic variables, including age, gender, professional qualification, area of working, years of experience, and source of information. Conclusion: The structured teaching programme was highly effective in improving the knowledge of staff nurses regarding surgical site infection and its prevention. These findings are consistent with the broader international literature, which similarly reports meaningful knowledge gains following structured educational interventions among nursing personnel. Enhancing nurses' knowledge through regular, structured educational programmes can strengthen infection prevention practices at the bedside and in the operation theatre, thereby contributing to a measurable reduction in the incidence of surgical site infections and an overall improvement in the quality and safety of patient care.

title: HBTC Framework: Hierarchical Biological Therapeutic Computation for Programmable Medicine - Spatial Transcriptomics & Kinetic Targeting
text:
HBTC Framework: Hierarchical Biological Therapeutic Computation for Programmable Medicine - Spatial Transcriptomics & Kinetic Targeting.   Comprehensive computational framework and bioinformatic pipeline for the HBTC Framework: Hierarchical Biological Therapeutic Computation for Programmable Medicine, integrating single-cell spatial transcriptomics with synthetic biology and programmatic nanotherapeutic delivery in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).  
     
  The repository and archive are structured into four sequential phases:  
  - Phase 1 (Documentation & Architectural Context): Theoretical foundations, technical abstracts, and translational specifications.  
  - Phase 2 (Computational Scripts & Source Code): Python source code for 10x Genomics Visium data preprocessing, Scanpy normalization, spatial co-expression correlation, niche validation, and Michaelis-Menten kinetic release simulations for the NP-B nanotherapeutic construct.  
  - Phase 3 (Tabular Data & Result Matrices): Processed marker genes, niche expression means, and nanoparticle release efficiency matrices.  
  - Phase 4 (Visualizations, Infographics & Final Reports): High-resolution UMAP clusters, H&E spatial overlaps, stacked violin plots, correlation heatmaps, and comprehensive standalone executive reports (PDF & HTML).  
     
  Primary Data Source: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), dataset accession GSE274103.

title: Cross-species animal-level pseudobulk analysis of mitochondrial transcriptional responses associated with prolonged sevoflurane exposure in the aged hippocampus: analysis code and derived results
journal: Wei, Zhuowen, Wu, Bin, Wang, Zhigao
text:
Cross-species animal-level pseudobulk analysis of mitochondrial transcriptional responses associated with prolonged sevoflurane exposure in the aged hippocampus: analysis code and derived results.  This record contains the analysis code, frozen gene-set definitions, accession-to-sample mappings, input hashes, one-to-one mouse-marmoset ortholog mappings, validation gates, software environment information, derived result tables, and output manifests supporting the study “Cross-species animal-level pseudobulk analysis of mitochondrial transcriptional responses associated with prolonged sevoflurane exposure in the aged hippocampus.” 
 The primary analysis treats animals rather than cells as biological replicates and evaluates 13 predefined gene sets in five shared cell types across GSE222430 and GSE234493. GSE303920 is included only as a same-animal alternative-processing sensitivity analysis, and GSE155770 is included only as a high-risk bulk boundary analysis. The release includes the complete 65-hypothesis primary family, matched-random-set evaluations, top-five gene deletion analyses, leave-one-animal-out analyses, and sensitivity tables including negative and non-testable results. 
 Raw GEO expression matrices are not redistributed and remain available from their original accession records. This deposit supports reproducibility of the computational analyses. Its RNA-level results do not establish mitochondrial functional change, ferroptosis, neurotoxicity, or causality. 
 Licensing is component-specific rather than an umbrella license for the archive: analysis scripts are under the MIT License; original documentation, figures, and derived statistical result tables are under CC BY 4.0; FerrDb-derived frozen content remains under CC BY-NC 4.0; and all other third-party-derived materials retain their source terms. title: INTESTINAL BARRIER DYSFUNCTION AND CONTROL OF ENDOGENOUS INTOXICATION IN ACUTE PANCREATITIS: OPPORTUNITIES FOR INTEGRATING ENTEROSORPTION INTO A CLINICAL ALGORITHM
journal: Kozimjonova Mumtozbegim Rustam qizi, Salokhiddinov K.Z., Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
text: INTESTINAL BARRIER DYSFUNCTION AND CONTROL OF ENDOGENOUS INTOXICATION IN ACUTE PANCREATITIS: OPPORTUNITIES FOR INTEGRATING ENTEROSORPTION INTO A CLINICAL ALGORITHM.     Background. Severe acute pancreatitis is driven not only by local pancreatic injury but also by systemic mediator release, impaired intestinal barrier integrity, and translocation of microbial products. Objective. To structure endogenous intoxication mechanisms along the pancreas-gut-systemic inflammation axis and define the potential role and limitations of enterosorption in multimodal care. Materials and methods. Eighteen key sources published in 2000-2026, including clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, experimental studies, and clinical reports, were assessed using a structured analytical approach. Results. Four linked components were identified: acinar injury, dysregulated mediator response, intestinal barrier failure, and secondary systemic endotoxemia. Sorbent binding of bacterial toxins and selected inflammatory mediators is mechanistically plausible; however, high-quality clinical evidence that oral enterosorption reduces mortality, organ failure, or infected necrosis is insufficient. Conclusion. Enterosorption cannot replace guideline-based fluid, nutritional, and etiologic treatment. It may be considered only as an adjunct in selected patients with preserved intestinal function and no contraindications, preferably within a research protocol or a locally approved clinical pathway.
